planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to dappled sun in spring; wood cranesbill is native to the cool woodlands and meadows of Europe and western Asia and tolerates more sun than most woodland geraniums where summers stay mild.

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to dappled sun in spring, working in compost to improve moisture retention in lean soils. Wood cranesbill forms a tidy mound of deeply lobed, softly hairy leaves topped in late spring to early summer by abundant violet-blue to purple-pink flowers with a small white eye. It tolerates more sun than most woodland geraniums in cooler climates but appreciates afternoon shade and consistent moisture where summers turn hot and humid. Shear the entire clump back by half after the main flush of bloom to tidy the foliage and often coax a lighter rebloom later in the season.

planting.note: Surface-sow; seed needs light to germinate. Established clumps spread steadily by rhizome and can also be divided in spring or fall.

directions: Surface-sow seed in fall or early spring, pressing it lightly into well-drained, fertile soil without covering, since light aids germination; established clumps can also be divided in spring or fall. Clustered bellflower produces dense, rounded clusters of upward-facing violet-purple bells packed tightly at the stem tips, a habit distinctive enough to have earned it the old common name Danesblood, and it spreads steadily by rhizome to form a substantial patch over a few seasons. Give it full sun to light afternoon shade and average, well-drained soil; it is more vigorous and spreading than most clump-forming bellflowers, so site it where its wandering habit is welcome or divide it regularly to keep it in bounds. Deadhead spent flower clusters to prolong bloom and prevent excessive self-seeding.

planting.note: Surface-sow; seed needs light to germinate. One of the tallest garden campanulas and may benefit from staking or the support of nearby plants.

directions: Surface-sow seed in early spring or fall, pressing it lightly onto well-drained, fertile soil without covering, or plant divisions from an established clump. Milky bellflower is one of the tallest garden campanulas, sending up sturdy, well-branched stems topped with airy, open clusters of pale lavender-blue, pink, or white bells from midsummer into fall, native to the mountains of the Caucasus and northern Turkey. It performs best in rich, evenly moist soil with full sun in cooler climates or afternoon shade where summers are hot, and larger cultivars often benefit from staking or the support of nearby plants to stay upright. Cut spent stems back hard after the first flush of bloom to encourage a second round of flowering into fall.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in well-drained soil; blooms later in the season and generally taller than the more commonly grown Veronica spicata.

directions: Plant divisions or container plants in average, well-drained soil in full sun in spring, spacing plants to allow good air circulation around the narrow, upright clumps. Garden speedwell produces long, slender leaves and tall, tapering spikes of violet-blue flowers from midsummer into early fall, blooming later and often taller than the more commonly grown Veronica spicata, making it a favored source of blue for late-season borders and cut-flower arrangements. It tolerates average garden soil and some drought once established but flowers most heavily with consistent moisture and a spring feeding. Deadhead spent spikes back to a lateral bud to extend bloom, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification and spring germination; alpine columbine is a compact, high-elevation species from the European Alps and resents hot, soggy lowland conditions.

directions: Direct sow in fall to allow winter cold to stratify the seed for spring germination, or start indoors after a period of cold, moist stratification, pressing seed lightly onto the soil surface without deep covering. Alpine columbine is a compact, high-elevation species from the European Alps, producing large, nodding, blue to violet-blue flowers with short, hooked spurs held above finely divided blue-green foliage, generally shorter and more richly colored than common garden columbines. It prefers full sun in cool, mountain-like climates but appreciates afternoon shade and sharply drained soil where summers are warm, since it resents the soggy, poorly drained conditions typical of lowland gardens. Like other columbines it is short-lived but self-seeds readily where happy, and seedlings may cross with other Aquilegia species growing nearby.
